title: Let Everything That Has Breath Praise the LORD
summary: The last psalm is a single sustained call to praise. It says where to praise God (in his sanctuary and his heavens), why (for his mighty acts and surpassing greatness), how (with horn, harp, lyre, tambourine, dancing, strings, flute, and cymbals), and who should do it: everything that has breath.
story: Psalm 150 closes the Book of Psalms. The Psalter began with a blessing on the one who meditates on God's instruction (Psalm 1) and with God's king installed on Zion (Psalm 2), and it has passed through lament, confession, exile, anger, doubt, thanksgiving, and hope. It ends not with a lament or a lesson but with thirteen commands to praise and a final Hallelujah. That ending is itself a statement: the prayers of God's people, even their bitterest complaints, are headed toward praise. Each of the Psalter's first four books ends with a short blessing of God (41:13, 72:18-19, 89:52, 106:48); Psalm 150 serves as the closing doxology of the fifth book and of the whole collection.
historical:
The psalm has no superscription, author, or occasion. Like Psalms 146 to 149, it is often dated to the period after the exile, when the Psalter was being gathered into its final form, and it was likely placed here deliberately by the editors who arranged the book. Its list of instruments reflects the music of the Second Temple, rebuilt after the return from Babylon and completed around 516 BC, where Levitical musicians led worship; 1 Chronicles 15 and 16 and 2 Chronicles 5 describe similar ensembles of trumpets, harps, lyres, and cymbals in the time of David and Solomon. The psalm itself, though, describes praise that spills beyond any one building or period.

In later worship Psalm 150 was sung with Psalms 145 to 149 in the Jewish daily morning service, and in the Christian daily office it was part of the morning praise sung at dawn. Its words have been set to music by composers in many eras.
cultural:
The instruments named would have been familiar sounds. The horn (shofar) was a ram's horn, blown to signal assemblies, festivals, the start of battle, and the coronation of a king; it gave a loud, piercing call rather than a melody. The harp and lyre were stringed instruments plucked by hand and used to accompany singing, the lyre being the instrument associated with David. The tambourine was a hand drum, often played by women at celebrations and dances. The strings and flute (or pipe) of verse 4 add more stringed and wind sounds, and verse 5 names two kinds of cymbals, perhaps a lighter and a louder pair.

What is striking is the range. The shofar belonged to priests and to public occasions, the harp and lyre to trained Levitical musicians, and the tambourine and dance to ordinary people in festive crowds. The psalm gathers the sacred and the popular, the solemn and the joyful, into one orchestra. Then it goes further: the final line names not an instrument but breath, the thing every living creature shares.
literary: The psalm is the simplest in structure of the whole book. Framed by Hallelujah at both ends, its body consists almost entirely of the command praise Him, repeated in each half-line. Verse 1 gives the place (sanctuary and heavens, earth and sky), verse 2 the reason (his mighty acts and his greatness), and verses 3 to 5 the means, a list of instruments that grows louder toward the resounding cymbals. Verse 6 breaks the pattern: instead of another praise Him with, it widens to “everything that has breath”. There is no request, no complaint, and no explanation beyond God himself. The repetition is the meaning: praise is the goal toward which the whole book has been moving.

outline.t: Where: in his sanctuary and in his heavens
Why: his mighty acts and surpassing greatness
How: with every instrument and with dancing

doctrines.note: The only reasons given for praise are God's mighty acts and his excellent greatness. The psalm doesn't praise God for what he gives so much as for who he is and what he has done, and it treats that as reason enough.
The final call goes to everything that has breath, the same gift God gave the first human being in Genesis 2:7. Every creature that lives by God's breath is called to return it to him in praise.

By ending the Psalter in pure praise after so many laments, the editors made a claim about where history is going. The cries of Psalms 13, 22, and 88 are real, but they are not the last word. The last word is praise.

words.note: Halal, to praise, appears thirteen times in six verses. It means to boast in or celebrate someone, to speak of their worth with enthusiasm. From this verb comes Hallelujah and also Tehillim, the Hebrew name of the Book of Psalms. The psalm is almost nothing but this word, which is exactly its point.

Neshamah, breath. This is the word for the breath of life God breathed into the first human (Genesis 2:7). It is the most basic sign of being alive. The Psalter's last call is addressed not only to priests or singers or Israel, but to every creature that breathes.

Shofar, the ram's horn. It announced festivals and the Day of Atonement, gathered the people, sounded in battle, and hailed new kings. Placing it first in the list of instruments gives the psalm the note of a royal proclamation: the King is being acclaimed.

christ: The New Testament shows where this universal call to praise is heading. In Revelation 5:13 every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea praises the one seated on the throne and the Lamb, the risen Christ. Paul writes that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10-11). The mighty acts for which Psalm 150 praises God find their greatest instance, in Christian faith, in the death and resurrection of Jesus. The psalm doesn't name him, and the connection is one of fulfillment rather than prediction: the praise of everything that breathes is gathered, in the New Testament's vision, around the Lamb.
questions: The Book of Psalms ends in praise after many laments. How does knowing where the book ends affect the way you read, or pray, its darker psalms?
Psalm 150 gives only God's acts and greatness as reasons for praise. What would it look like to praise God for who he is rather than only for what you have received?
The psalm brings together the priest's horn, the Levite's harp, and the crowd's tambourine. What does that suggest about the variety of worship God welcomes?
